The 4 vehicle families at a glance

India's major launch vehicles are distinguished by their propulsion configurations, payload classes and usual mission requirements. Their names provide a useful starting point, but the actual spacecraft mass and required orbit determine which missions a vehicle can undertake.

VehiclePropulsion stagesIndicative payload capacityPrincipal association
PSLV4: solid, liquid, solid, liquid1,750 kg to 600 km SSPOPolar and Sun-synchronous missions; versatile satellite launches
GSLV Mk II3: solid core with liquid strap-ons; liquid; cryogenic2,250 kg to GTOCommunication and navigation satellites; transfer-orbit missions
LVM33: solid boosters; liquid core; cryogenic4,000 kg to GTO; 8,000 kg to 600 km LEOHeavy satellites, commercial constellations and lunar missions
SSLV3 solid stages plus liquid VTM500 kg to 500 km planar LEODedicated small-satellite launches

All capacity figures are approximate reference values from ISRO's vehicle specifications. The orbit attached to each number is part of the fact: 1,750 kg to SSPO and 2,250 kg to GTO cannot be treated as capacities measured under identical conditions.

How to distinguish the propulsion systems

PSLV is the only vehicle among these 4 with the characteristic sequence of 4 alternating solid and liquid stages. GSLV Mk II and LVM3 both use cryogenic upper stages, but GSLV Mk II uses CE-7.5 while LVM3 uses CE-20. SSLV has 3 solid stages and a separate liquid-based velocity trimming module.

Another difference concerns the early propulsion arrangement. PSLV's optional strap-on motors are solid. GSLV Mk II's 4 strap-on boosters are liquid. LVM3 starts with 2 large solid S200 boosters.

Four quick distinctions

  • PSLV: 4 alternating solid-liquid stages.
  • GSLV Mk II: 3 stages, 4 liquid strap-ons and CE-7.5 cryogenic engine.
  • LVM3: Heavy-lift rocket, 2 S200 solid boosters and CE-20 cryogenic engine.
  • SSLV: 3 solid stages followed by a liquid velocity trimming module.

Match the important missions with their launch vehicles

Mission names are often easier to remember when connected to a clear reason for the vehicle's selection.

  • Chandrayaan-1, 2008: Launched by PSLV-C11. PSLV supplied the initial launch for India's first lunar mission.
  • Mars Orbiter Mission, 2013: Launched by PSLV-C25. The spacecraft subsequently travelled from Earth orbit towards Mars.
  • AstroSat, 2015: Launched by PSLV-C30 as an astronomical-observation mission.
  • PSLV-C37, 2017: Carried 104 satellites into a polar Sun-synchronous orbit.
  • Chandrayaan-2, 2019: Launched by LVM3-M1, then still commonly designated GSLV Mk III.
  • Chandrayaan-3, 2023: Launched by LVM3-M4.
  • Aditya-L1, 2023: Launched by PSLV-C57.
  • EOS-08, 2024: Launched by SSLV-D3.
  • NISAR, 2025: Launched by GSLV-F16 into a Sun-synchronous polar orbit.
  • NVS-03, 2026: Launched by GSLV-F18 into GTO.

These examples demonstrate why the vehicle's name alone is an unreliable guide to the final mission destination. PSLV has launched spacecraft that later travelled towards other celestial destinations, GSLV has launched a polar Earth-observation mission, and LVM3 has carried both lunar spacecraft and LEO communication constellations.

Important chronological milestones

Several dates mark different achievements and should not be confused. PSLV's first successful flight was in 1994, following its unsuccessful first developmental flight in 1993. GSLV's programme began flying in 2001, while a successful GSLV flight with an indigenous cryogenic upper stage came in 2014. LVM3's first orbital developmental flight occurred in 2017. SSLV's successful second developmental flight occurred in 2023, and its development project concluded after the successful third flight in 2024.

What is Gujarat's connection with India's space programme?

Space Applications Centre (SAC), an important ISRO centre, is located in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. Its work includes the development of spaceborne and airborne instruments and payloads, along with applications relating to communication, navigation and remote sensing.

Such instruments make satellites useful after launch. For example, Earth-observation payloads collect information that can support agricultural monitoring, land-use mapping, water-resource assessment and other public applications. Communication payloads support services such as television broadcasting and telecommunications.

SAC has contributed to Indian satellite programmes and scientific missions, including Chandrayaan-1 and the Mars Orbiter Mission. Thus, Gujarat has a genuine role in India's space programme through payload development and space applications.

The location of a space-applications centre must not be confused with the location of a major launch site. The launches discussed in this lesson took place from Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC SHAR), Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. SAC is in Ahmedabad; SDSC SHAR is in Sriharikota.

Distinctions that prevent incorrect answers

Launch success and mission success

A launch vehicle may successfully place a satellite into its assigned transfer orbit even if the satellite later encounters a propulsion problem. The GSLV-F15/NVS-02 mission is a useful example: the launcher successfully completed GTO insertion, but subsequent spacecraft orbit raising could not be completed.

The vehicle does not always reach the spacecraft's final destination

For Chandrayaan or Mars missions, the launch vehicle supplies the initial departure conditions. The spacecraft then uses its own systems and orbital manoeuvres to travel onward. Similarly, successful GTO insertion is usually followed by spacecraft manoeuvres before geostationary operation can begin.

Stage count is not the same as engine or booster count

GSLV Mk II has 4 liquid strap-on motors but only 3 sequential stages. LVM3 has 2 large solid boosters but only 3 propulsion stages. SSLV has 3 solid stages and a separate liquid terminal module. PSLV has 4 sequential stages even when the number of strap-on boosters changes.

Names and actual orbits must be checked separately

PSLV is not restricted to polar orbits, and GSLV is not restricted to geosynchronous transfer orbits. The destination depends on the flight plan and vehicle capability. The actual orbital parameters of a named mission provide a more reliable answer than assumptions drawn from the launch vehicle's abbreviation.

Prelims focus

  • PSLV has 4 alternating solid-liquid stages; GSLV Mk II, LVM3 and SSLV each have 3 principal propulsion stages.
  • GSLV Mk II uses CE-7.5; LVM3 uses CE-20.
  • Chandrayaan-1 and the Mars Orbiter Mission used PSLV; Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3 used LVM3.
  • SSLV-D3/EOS-08 completed SSLV's developmental programme in 2024.
  • SAC is located in Ahmedabad, Gujarat; SDSC SHAR is located at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh.
  • Trap: Always compare payload capacities for the same specified orbit and distinguish rocket insertion from later spacecraft manoeuvres.
